# Why Dharma belongs in your address bar

Every address bar is a choice. When you type ​**Dharma**, you are not typing a novelty; you are restoring a name that the early DNS, built for English typewriters, could not carry. The plain ASCII form *dharma* is a leftover of that ‌constraint, not the name itself. This post is the long version of the restoration: where the name comes from, how the Devanagari tradition wrote it, how it is pronounced, what the myths and ‌the material record preserve, and why its Unicode form now lives as a working domain. The claim throughout is simple — the original spelling is not decoration. It is the name.

## At a ​Glance

- **Restored name:** Dharma
- **ASCII form:** dharma
- **Meaning:** "That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain')."
- **Domain ​of influence:** Law, Duty, Righteousness
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** धर्म (Devanagari)

## Overview

**Dharma** (*dharma*) — That Which Holds, Law and Righteousness · That which holds or sustains — law, duty, ​and righteousness — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Law, Duty, Righteousness". The name means "That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness; the moral ​and religious order that upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain').".

**Dharma** is the load-bearing word of Indian civilization: the law that holds the cosmos, the duty that holds the person, the ​order that holds society. From √dhṛ, ‘to sustain’, it names everything that keeps the world from sliding into chaos — and in the epics it walks as a person: the god of righteousness, ‌father of Yudhiṣṭhira, who came down to test his own devotees.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Dharma** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/dharma/). The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from ​the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *dharma* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically ​complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Devanagari as **धर्म**. Etymologically it means "That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that upholds the world ‌(from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain').".

The ASCII form *dharma* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Dharma** ​recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration aSCII-equivalent form — a description computed from the displayed form itself.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **d** → ‌**D** — Same, capitalized
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **m** → **m** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

## The Original Script

The ​name is preserved in Devanagari as **धर्म**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Dharma*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Dharma is written in Devanagari as धर्म
- IAST transliteration maps each Devanagari vowel ‌and consonant to a Latin equivalent
- Macrons mark long vowels (ā, ī, ū); dots beneath consonants mark retroflex articulation (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ)

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈdɑːrmə/** — ​Sanskrit (IAST: Dharma).

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Dhar-** — The dh is a voiced aspirate — “d” with breath; the a is long “ah”.
- **-ma** — The word is the abstract noun from √dhṛ, ​“to hold, sustain” — that which holds the world up.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: “DAHR-muh”

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Pāli** — Dhamma
- **Avestan** — daēnā (cognate ​family)

Not a god but a principle — personified as a god in the epics, whence this entry. In compounds the stem appears as dharma-; Middle Indic shortens it to dhamma-.

## Mythology

Dharma’s ​mythology is the epics’ moral machinery: the god of righteousness fathers the eldest Pāṇḍava, tests his devotees in disguise, and — in the Nala story — teaches dice to a king as the ​instrument of ruin. He has no cult-image because he is what every cult-image stands for; yet the tradition gave him a family and a biography.

### The Father of Yudhiṣṭhira (Mahābhārata)

When Pāṇḍu was ‌cursed to die on his wedding night, his queens invoked the gods: Dharmarāja himself, the god of righteousness, fathered Yudhiṣṭhira on Kuntī. The eldest Pāṇḍava is thus dharma’s son — which is why ​the epic keeps asking whether righteousness itself can survive the dice-game and the war it forces.

### The Tests in Disguise (Dharma-Upākhyāna)

The epic’s forest-books stage Dharma’s examinations: as a stork demanding why Yudhiṣṭhira ‌would not abandon a fallen brother; as a Yakṣa whose riddles the king answers with the epic’s most quoted verses; as a dog who follows the Pāṇḍavas to heaven’s gate and is refused ​entry — until Yudhiṣṭhira refuses heaven without it. The dog was Dharma; the gate opens.

### The God Who Taught Dice (Nala Cycle)

In the Nala episode, Kali — the demon of the Kali ‌Yuga — begs Dharma for a means to enter the righteous king Nala; Dharma, inexplicably, teaches him dice. The story’s commentators wrestled for centuries with the god of righteousness arming the demon of ​strife: the standard resolution — even dharma’s permission is a test that righteousness must survive.

### The Son of Brahmā (Purāṇic Personification)

The Purāṇas give Dharma genealogy: born of Brahmā’s breast as one of ‌the mind-born sons, husband of Dhṛti and father of the personified virtues — Kāma (desire), Lobha (greed), Darpa (pride) and the rest. The abstraction’s family-tree is the Indian psyche’s map of its own ​forces.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Dharma concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The Load-Bearer** — The cosmos rests on dharma; the ‌four feet of the bull of dharma mark the four ages of time.
- **Duty by Caste and Stage** — Svadharma — one’s own duty by birth and life-stage: the Bhagavadgītā’s central teaching.
- **The ​Cosmic Ages** — The four yugas are the four feet of the bull: four in the Kṛta age, one stumbling foot in ours.
- **The Tester of Men** — In the epics Dharma appears ​in disguise — a beggar, a dog, a crane — to test righteousness where it counts.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The material record for Dharma survives in a small number of securely identified remains, ‌catalogued below; the corpus is thin but unambiguous, and each site is tied to the name by ancient testimony.

Dharma’s monuments are juridical: the edict-pillars of Aśoka, whose dhamma inscriptions are the oldest ‌deciphered moral legislation on earth. His wheel crowns the Indian flag; his bull — the dharmavṛṣabha — kneels on the seal of the Republic.

## Realm & Domain

**Dharma** is the load-bearing word of ‌Indian civilization: the law that holds the cosmos, the duty that holds the person, the order that holds society. From √dhṛ, ‘to sustain’, it names everything that keeps the world from sliding into ​chaos — and in the epics it walks as a person: the god of righteousness, father of Yudhiṣṭhira, who came down to test his own devotees.

### The Load-Bearer

The cosmos rests on dharma; ​the four feet of the bull of dharma mark the four ages of time.

### Duty by Caste and Stage

Svadharma — one’s own duty by birth and life-stage: the Bhagavadgītā’s central teaching.

### The ‌Cosmic Ages

The four yugas are the four feet of the bull: four in the Kṛta age, one stumbling foot in ours.

### The Tester of Men

In the epics Dharma appears in disguise ​— a beggar, a dog, a crane — to test righteousness where it counts.

## Across Cultures

Dharma and the Buddha’s Dhamma share a word and a mission: the Buddha claimed the title Dharmarāja, ​king of the law, and made dharma’s wheel — the dharmacakra — his teaching’s emblem. The Zoroastrian daēnā and the Roman Fas are the comparison-points scholars cite; in India itself dharma absorbed every ‌local law-code, from the Vedic ṛta to the medieval digests.

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[aditi|Aditi]], [[agni|Agni]], [[ambika|Ambikā]], [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[arjuna|Arjuna]], and [[bhakti|Bhakti]].

## Cultural Legacy

The word is ​untranslatable and indispensable — every rendering (‘law’, ‘duty’, ‘religion’, ‘righteousness’) is a fraction. The four feet of dharma’s bull are India’s theory of history; the Bhagavadgītā’s ‘better one’s own dharma, though defective’ is ​among the most quoted ethical sentences on earth. India’s modern name for itself, ‘Hindu Dharma’, keeps the word at the nation’s centre.

## The Scholarly Record

The account of Dharma given in this edition ‌rests on the witnesses and reference works listed below. Lexica and etymological dictionaries secure the form and meaning of the name; the literary and religious texts supply the narrative evidence.

-  Mahābhārata (Dharma-Upākhyāna ​cycle).
-  Bhagavadgītā 3.35 (svadharma verse).
-  Nala episode, Vana Parvan.
-  Purāṇic genealogies of the mind-born sons.

## A Meditation

Dharma: the name of the thing that holds, restored in letters that hold nothing but carry ‌everything. It needs no mark over its vowels — the word’s burden is its own diacritic, the weight of the worlds it has held for four thousand years.

## The Unicode Restoration

Dharma aSCII-equivalent ​form. The ASCII fallback *dharma* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

**Which tradition does Dharma belong to?** Dharma is catalogued in the Sanskrit pantheon of the PuniCodex lexicon.

**What does Dharma preserve that ASCII cannot show?** The form itself answers: Dharma aSCII-equivalent ​form — and the marks in the restored spelling are exactly that evidence.

**Can I use Dharma in a normal browser?** Yes. The DNS resolves the punycode form automatically, and the type tool ‌on this site converts dharma to Dharma for copying and pasting.

**Where does the scholarly information come from?** The entry is built from lexica, inscriptional evidence, and reviewed scholarly sources listed in the ​Scholarly Edition. Every claim is traceable to a canonical source.

## Why This Restoration ‌Matters

Restoring **Dharma** is part of a larger effort to make the web multilingual by default. The PuniCodex project does not ask users to learn a new alphabet; it asks the infrastructure to ‌respect the alphabets that already exist. Every section of this post — the script, the sound, the myths, the evidence — converges on the same point: the marks in Dharma are information, and ‌information deserves an address of its own. A single Unicode domain is a small proof, but it is a proof that scales: every name restored makes the next one easier, and every visit ​to the temple is a vote for the restored form.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Dharma**, the map does not lead ​through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Devanagari rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *dharma* and the restored form share the same letters; the ​restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully ‌reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still ​lists each character — **d**, **h**, **a**, **r**, **m**, **a** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, ​a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

## Dharma in Its Tradition

**Dharma** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is counted among 102 names ​in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Law, Duty, Righteousness — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it ‌is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Dharma**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in ​a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, ​between a tradition and a trend. **Dharma** is one such vote.

## The Restoration on the Live Web

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Dharma** ​resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone ‌who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. Before Unicode domains, a scholar could write the name correctly in an ​article while the public web flattened it to *dharma*. Now the public web can carry the correct form end to end. The punycode translation happens silently, so the infrastructure remains compatible while the ‌visible name keeps its marks. That compromise — human-readable restoration, machine-readable encoding — is the foundation of every PuniCodex temple.

## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a ‌sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Dharma**, the chain begins with the attested form in Devanagari, continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the ​DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "That which holds or sustains — law, duty, and righteousness; the moral and religious order that upholds the world (from √dhṛ, 'to hold, sustain')." ​anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Dharma** and the ASCII form *dharma* share the same Latin ​letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the restoration logic the displayed form wears ​openly: Dharma aSCII-equivalent form. The rule is mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see ‌exactly which evidence produced it, because every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, ‌not invented.
